L9@P1: Operation “Pedestal”, Convoy to Malta, 11-15 August 1942
L10@P1: with particular reference to
L11@P1: the strategic value of Malta in the Mediterranean during the Second World War
L12@P1: Malta in the Early War Years of World War II
L13@P1: During the inter-war years Malta was used as a main fleet base for the Mediterranean Fleet,
L14@P1: as it lay astride the main Imperial routes to the Middle and Far East theatres and provided a
L15@P1: well-placed forward striking base for use against Italian submarines, as was suggested by
L16@P1: Admiral of the Fleet, Dudley Pound in 1938.1
L17@P1:  This view, echoing the strategic ideas from the
L18@P1: First World War, took little account of the rise of air power.
L19@P1: After Italy entered the war, Malta ceased to be a main fleet base, due to the close proximity
L20@P1: of Italian air power which made it too vulnerable. British naval forces were then divided into
L21@P1: two: the main portion, the Mediterranean Fleet, being based at Alexandria with a smaller
L22@P1: British detachment, known as Force “H”, based at Gibraltar able to operate in the Western
L23@P1: Mediterranean and North Atlantic.2
L24@P1:  Malta remained the lynch pin which connected these two
L25@P1: strategic areas of the Mediterranean theatre.3
L26@P1: With the abandonment of the central Mediterranean as a main fleet area, the Mediterranean
L27@P1: was effectively closed for the passage of merchant shipping to the Far East via the Suez
L28@P1: Canal. For the British, her forces in the Middle East had to be supplied from Australia, India,
L29@P1: South Africa and, mainly, from the United Kingdom or North America. The latter distance to
L30@P1: the Canal Zone being about 14,000 miles. Even so, the WS Convoys which plied this route
L31@P1: were often delayed but almost all arrived safely. Indeed only one ship was lost in these
L32@P1: convoys.4
L33@P1:  Of the many cargoes carried to the Middle East in British convoys barely 3% of
L34@P1: them were lost to enemy action. The Axis forces, on the other hand, had to send supplies for
L35@P1: their forces in North Africa over just 600 miles across the Mediterranean, but the whole of
L36@P1: this passage was within the striking distance of British aircraft, submarines and surface ships
L37@P1: based at Malta and the enemy lost, by their own estimate, over 16% of embarked cargoes.5
L38@P1: To put the figures in wider context, when Italy entered the war, she lost about one-third of
L39@P1: her merchant marine when ships were seized in ports outside the Mediterranean. By
L40@P1: September 1942 about one-half of the remainder had been destroyed in the Mediterranean
L41@P1: by British striking forces. This substantially reduced her ability to re-supply the Axis forces in
L42@P1: North Africa, particularly during periods when the Axis needed to surge reinforcements of
L43@P1: men or supplies to meet major operations in the Western Desert.
L44@P1: The area covered by the joint RN and RAF air striking force is illustrated in the map below.

L67@P2: Apart from its offensive value lying athwart the Axis lines of communication to North Africa,
L68@P2: Malta was also an essential staging post for larger aircraft on the air reinforcement route to
L69@P2: the Middle East and India. In a post war lecture it was noted that:–
L70@P2: When the history of the war comes to be written, it will be generally recognised that the
L71@P2: maintenance of Malta, as a base for offensive operations, was the “Corner Stone” on
L72@P2: which the whole strategy of the war in the Mediterranean has been built. The success of
L73@P2: its air and submarine offensive in the last months of 1941, and from July onwards of
L74@P2: 1942, played a decisive part in those Military successes in Libya and North Africa which
L75@P2: have culminated in the tremendous victory in Tunisia. Malta’s contribution to the
L76@P2: destruction of the Axis air strength alone is impressive: 1,000 enemy aircraft have been
L77@P2: shot down by the fighters and A/A gunfire of the Island. …6
L78@P2: Award of the George Cross to Malta
L79@P2: After the heavy air attacks on Malta throughout the spring of 1942, King George VI bestowed
L80@P2: the George Cross on the Island on 15 April 1942, so as to “bear witness to the heroism and
L81@P2: devotion of its people.”7
L82@P2:  The news of the award appeared in the newspapers in Malta two
L83@P2: days later, and the medal itself was flown to the island on 7 May 1942 in a Coastal

L94@P3: June 1942 Convoys to Malta
L95@P3: An attempt to run a re-supply convoy, MG 1, through to Malta from Alexandria in March 1942
L96@P3: ended in failure with barely one-fifth of the embarked cargoes being off-loaded in Malta.
L97@P3: However, the passage of the Convoy had brought on an action between the light cruisers of
L98@P3: Rear Admiral Philip Vian’s covering force and the Italian Fleet’s heavy ships during which the
L99@P3: Royal Navy, though out-numbered and out-gunned, nevertheless gained a victory and forced
L100@P3: the Italians to retreat. Following on from the earlier offensive strikes at Taranto and Cape
L101@P3: Matapan, this Second Battle of Sirte sealed the psychological dominance of the Royal Navy
L102@P3: over their Italian adversaries for months to come.
L103@P3: It was decided not to run a convoy through to Malta from the west for the time being, but the
L104@P3: Governor of Malta felt it necessary to point out that:
L105@P3: …our situation is so grave that it is my duty to restate in the clearest possible terms. The
L106@P3: decision materially reduces our chances of survival not because of any failure of morale
L107@P3: or fighting efficiency but because it is impossible to carry on without food and
L108@P3: ammunition. …The position with regard to these is as follows:–
L109@P3: (A) Flour. We have enough to last until the later half of May….
L110@P3: (B) A/A Ammunition…we have slightly over a month’s supply….9
L111@P3: In the interim several RN submarines and fast ships were pressed into service to run
L112@P3: supplies into the Island. In June 1942 there was an attempt to carry out a large-scale
L113@P3: resupply of Malta with two convoys, “Harpoon” from the Gibraltar end and “Vigorous” from
L114@P3: Alexandria. The latter failed completely and none of its 11 supply ships got through, due to
L115@P3: the threat from the Italian Battle Fleet which delayed the westerly progress of the convoy and
L116@P3: incessant air attacks which absorbed almost all the escorts’ anti-aircraft ammunition.
L117@P3: However, 2 out of 6 ships of eastbound “Harpoon” Convoy got through to the island.10 With
L118@P3: the meagre 15,000 tons of the stores landed it was estimated that, provided there was a
L119@P3: good harvest, the Island’s supplies would then last until September. Consequently it was
L120@P3: decided in London that no attempt would be made to run another convoy in July, reserving
L121@P3: the naval forces for a Convoy to Russia in June-July 1942).11 But, in the opinion of Lord
L122@P3: Gort, the Governor and Supreme Commander in Malta, the stocks of aviation spirit were
L123@P3: being used up too quickly. If resistance was to be prolonged for as much as possible, these
L124@P3: stocks would need to be replenished soon in order to sustain the defending RAF fighter
L125@P3: force. However, during the first weeks of July, the RAF had lost 36 out of 135 Spitfires based
L126@P3: on the island while repulsing renewed Axis air attacks. The continuing shortage of aviation
L127@P3: fuel also affected the Island’s air striking force’s ability to operate effectively against
L128@P3: Rommel’s supply lines across the central Mediterranean basin.12

L141@P4: The problem of deciding the allocation of fuel between the air defence of Malta and the
L142@P4: operation of its air striking force was to a large extent governed by the situation in the land
L143@P4: battles in North Africa. The Eighth Army had begun its withdrawal from the Gazala position
L144@P4: while Operations “Harpoon” and “Vigorous” were running and these convoys attracted a high
L145@P4: proportion of the Axis air power that would, otherwise, have been directed against the Eighth
L146@P4: Army’s well-ordered retreat (and which might have turned the withdrawal into a rout).13 A few
L147@P4: days after the convoy operations ended Tobruk had fallen and by the end of June the enemy
L148@P4: were in possession of Mersa Matruh about 160 miles from Alexandria. As a direct result of
L149@P4: the air threat and possible ground occupation of Alexandria, the Commander-in-Chief,
L150@P4: Mediterranean, Admiral Harwood, decided to disperse what remained of the Mediterranean
L151@P4: Fleet to ports in the Eastern Mediterranean and to the south of the Canal. Nevertheless,
L152@P4: some of the offensive parts of the Fleet remained to assist the Army by carrying out
L153@P4: bombardments of enemy positions around Mersa Matruh.14 Worse still, for the prospects of
L154@P4: the defence of Malta from Axis air attack, with the 8th Army now forced back towards the
L155@P4: Canal Zone and the airfields near Benghazi and Derna in enemy hands, it was no longer
L156@P4: possible to fly in to Malta single-engined fighters, such as Spitfires, from the east. Inserting
L157@P4: these aircraft from the west meant using aircraft carriers and this would require a special
L158@P4: naval operation.
L159@P4: With the rapid advance of the Afrika Korps and the consequent loss of airfields in Cyrenaica,
L160@P4: further convoys to Malta from the Eastern Mediterranean would be very difficult to mount
L161@P4: because the Desert Air Force would be unable to provide much by way of fighter protection
L162@P4: for the Mediterranean Fleet, itself now denuded of all its aircraft carriers. The loss of these
L163@P4: airfields also meant that the Desert Air Force’s ability to interdict Axis supply lines was
L164@P4: restricted to the use of the few long-range bombers available. It was fortunate, therefore, that
L165@P4: the small number of RAF long-range bombers was augmented by a small detachment of
L166@P4: United States Army Air Force (USAAF) Liberators, the Halverson Project, which had recently
L167@P4: arrived in the Middle East and, with the agreement of Washington, were held in the area
L168@P4: from June 1942 until early the following year. Having carried out a raid on the Roumanian oil
L169@P4: refineries at Ploesti, these USAAF aircraft were used to support Operation “Vigorous” and
L170@P4: subsequently to carry out long-range bombing missions against Axis supply ports in North
L171@P4: Africa.15
L172@P4: The Prime Minister thought that the loss of Malta ‘…would be a disaster of [the] first
L173@P4: magnitude to the British Empire, and probably [would be] fatal in the long run to the defence
L174@P4: of the Nile Valley.’16 The heavy losses suffered during the June Mediterranean convoys and
L175@P4: the small quantity of cargo delivered in no way weakened the Government’s or the
L176@P4: Admiralty’s resolve to keep Malta supplied. Both were determined to attempt a further
L177@P4: resupply operation, even if further heavy losses were incurred. Though it might be noted that
L178@P4: the British Chiefs of Staff were of the opinion that it was finely balanced whether the correct

L199@P5: Operation “Pedestal” – The Plan
L200@P5: Experience of the June convoys to Malta made it clear that any attempt from the east was
L201@P5: almost certainly doomed to failure, given the weakness of the Mediterranean Fleet and the
L202@P5: loss of the RAF airfields in Cyrenaica (from which air protection could be provided for the
L203@P5: passage of the convoys to Malta) due to the advance of Rommel’s Afrika Corps to within 90
L204@P5: miles of Alexandria.18 Instead, the plan for an August convoy, WS 12S, codenamed
L205@P5: Operation “Pedestal”, was for a more than usually powerful escort to be assembled to escort
L206@P5: a single convoy of 14 fast merchant ships, which would include the fast tanker Ohio, through
L207@P5: to Malta from the west during the moonless period in the middle of the month. A small
L208@P5: diversionary convoy, Operation “Ascendant”, would be run part of the way from the Eastern
L209@P5: Mediterranean. With this considerable naval force being assembled for “Pedestal” it was not
L210@P5: possible to run an August convoy to Russia simultaneously.19
L211@P5: Vice Admiral E.N. Syfret, on his way home from the successful operations which resulted in
L212@P5: the occupation of the Vichy French base at Diego Suarez in May 1942, was ordered to
L213@P5: disembark at Takoradi in West Africa and fly home directly. Once in the UK he learned that
L214@P5: he was to command “Pedestal”, and on 13 July 1942 planning started in earnest for the
L215@P5: operation. The key was the provision of adequate air protection for the convoy and three
L216@P5: fleet carriers were to be allocated to Operation “Pedestal”.
L217@P5: To gather these carriers together it was decided to withdraw one of the three carriers in
L218@P5: Admiral Somerville’s Eastern Fleet, because the Admiralty assessed that the risk of a
L219@P5: Japanese foray into the Indian Ocean, similar to that of the previous Spring, was unlikely
L220@P5: after the American victory at Midway and the drawn battles around the Solomons. As a
L221@P5: result, Indomitable was withdrawn after completing the operations to capture Madagascar
L222@P5: from its Vichy French garrison. Also, after the loss of two thirds of the ships from the Arctic
L223@P5: Convoy PQ 17 in July, it had been decided to temporarily suspend these convoys. This
L224@P5: released the heavy ships of the Home Fleet to take part in “Pedestal” and, in particular, the
L225@P5: carrier Victorious. HMS Eagle was already, so to speak, in situ as part of Force “H” at
L226@P5: Gibraltar. Thus elements of world-wide deployed forces were to be concentrated to execute
L227@P5: Operation “Pedestal”.
L228@P5: The three aircraft carriers which would form part of the close protection of the convoy were:
L229@P5: Victorious, Flag of Rear Admiral Lyster, Rear Admiral (Aircraft Carriers, Home Fleet) (and
L230@P5: the architect and executor of the Taranto attack in 1940), Indomitable and Eagle. Between
L231@P5: them, they were to carry 72 fighters (Hurricanes, Martlets and Fulmars) as well as 28
L232@P5: Albacores for surface search, antisubmarine protection and as a small striking force.20 The
L233@P5: main naval forces were split into:

L252@P6: As this force approached Malta they would be met by minesweepers from the Island to take
L253@P6: them in though the enemy minefields sown to seaward of Grand Harbour.22 Meanwhile, the
L254@P6: subsidiary diversionary convoy operation codenamed “Ascendant” was also planned under
L255@P6: the cover provided by the main convoy to bring out the two merchant ships which had
L256@P6: arrived in Malta from the “Harpoon” convoy.23 At the last moment, the carrier Furious was
L257@P6: included in the convoy. She was to fly off 38 Spitfires to Malta (this formed Operation
L258@P6: “Bellows”) before returning to Gibraltar. Air defence of the convoy would be provided by the
L259@P6: three carriers until the Convoy was close enough to Malta for Air Vice Marshal Keith Park (of
L260@P6: Battle of Britain fame) to despatch first RAF long-range Beaufighters and then singleengined fighters to take over the protection of the convoy. At the same time, Park would
L261@P6: have some of the Island’s torpedo-bomber striking force on standby to attack the Italian fleet
L262@P6: should it close the convoy.
L263@P6: Throughout the operation, more distant protection was provided by eight RN submarines
L264@P6: deployed off the north coast of Sicily and further east. These submarines were to spend
L265@P6: some of their time on the surface, in order that enemy aircraft would report their position and,
L266@P6: hopefully, deter the intervention of the Italian fleet.24 During the “Vigorous” operation British
L267@P6: and French commandos had been landed from a submarine on Crete with the intention of
L268@P6: raiding the airfields there from which the enemy could attack the convoy. Some aircraft,
L269@P6: bombs and petrol destroyed. A similar attempt was made to lessen the weight of enemy
L270@P6: attack before the arrival of “Pedestal”, but it was unsuccessful.25
L271@P6: Operation “Berserk” – Operation “Pedestal” Work-up
L272@P6: On 31 July 1942 the first of the ships sailed from Scapa Flow. This force included the aircraft
L273@P6: carrier Argus which was to take part in the work-up, “Berserk”, but then played no part in the
L274@P6: main operation. “Berserk” was then carried out in the area to the west of the Gibraltar Straits
L275@P6: and involved all four carriers (i.e. including Argus) especially in Fighter Direction exercises.
L276@P6: Before the operations began, these ships, along with a fifth carrier, Argus, and the rest of the
L277@P6: force consisting of battleships, cruisers, destroyers, corvettes and oilers, carried out a series
L278@P6: of exercises, known as Operation “Berserk”, to the west of Gibraltar on 5-10 August 1942.

L299@P7: During this phase there were several irritating changes of detail to the operational plan,
L300@P7: which meant considerable signalling within the fleet at sea and with the shore authorities.
L301@P7: Not the least of these changes was brought about by the inclement weather in the Atlantic,
L302@P7: which prevented many of the ships from refuelling from the attendant tankers and this
L303@P7: resulted in those ships being sent into Gibraltar to top up with fuel. It was especially
L304@P7: important to fuel the ships as they entered the Mediterranean, for Malta had no fuel to

L342@P8: Just after noon, Furious hauled out of the convoy, taking with her an escort of destroyers,

L397@P10: Passage of “Pedestal” to Malta – Thursday, 13 August 1942 35
L398@P10: By midnight as the convoy passed Cape Bon, they entered the territory of enemy motor
L399@P10: torpedo-boats, or E-boats. In the early hours the cruiser Manchester was hit and brought to a
L400@P10: stop. The captain decided that his ship could not be salved and ordered her to be sunk, with
L401@P10: the crew making their way to the Tunisian coast.36 Also five of the merchant ships were hit,
L402@P10: four of them sinking during the night. As the Official Historian remarks: “…it was a cruel blow
L403@P10: suddenly to suffer such large casualties, after the convoy had come so far with such
L404@P10: success.”37
L405@P10: Soon after daylight the enemy bombers reappeared and another merchant ship was hit and
L406@P10: blew up, and the tanker Ohio was again damaged, this time by the aircraft attacking her
L407@P10: crashing into the ship! Although by late morning RAF Beaufighters and long-range Spitfires
L408@P10: were patrolling overhead, Ohio was again hit and this time disabled, while two other
L409@P10: merchant ships were seriously damaged. There were only three surviving merchant ships,
L410@P10: Port Chalmers, Melbourne Star and Rochester Castle, each struggling towards Malta, now
L411@P10: under the protection of the short-range Spitfires from the Island. They entered harbour at
L412@P10: about 1630 that afternoon. Three more damaged ships, Ohio, Dorset and Brisbane Star
L413@P10: were still some distance from Malta but great efforts were being made to get them in. Some
L414@P10: of these attempts were frustrated, for Dorset was again hit and later sank. Brisbane Star
L415@P10: however managed to struggle into Malta.
L416@P10: The destroyer Penn, and the minesweepers Rye and Ledbury took it in turns to fight off
L417@P10: further enemy attacks and to tow Ohio to Malta. Their efforts were met with success when
L418@P10: the tanker finally entered Grand Harbour on the morning of 15 August 1942, by which time
L419@P10: four other merchant ships from the convoy had been brought in. This day was traditionally
L420@P10: known in the Island as the feast of Santa Maria, and the “Pedestal” convoy has been called
L421@P10: the “Convoy of Santa Maria”.

L435@P11: Role of Ohio
L436@P11: The arrival of the four surviving ships of the “Pedestal” convoy ensured that Malta had the
L437@P11: supplies to maintain her defences for another few months. But more significant to the overall
L438@P11: situation in the Mediterranean was the arrival of the tanker Ohio. Her cargo was the critical to
L439@P11: the future of Malta’s strategic value as a striking base.38
L440@P11: The fuel which she carried enabled air strikes to be restarted from Malta just when
L441@P11: Rommel was preparing for the offensive intended to drive the Allies finally out of Egypt.
L442@P11: The enemy’s shipping losses to air attacks at once increased, and the offensive had to
L443@P11: be postponed because of shortage of supplies.39
L444@P11: For this reason, the fame of the tanker Ohio is rightly centred on her role in the “Pedestal”
L445@P11: convoy. However, she has a further claim. At the beginning of 1942, it was apparent to the
L446@P11: British that, although oil stocks in the country stood at a wartime high, the tempo of future
L447@P11: operations would rapidly run down these stocks. It seemed, however, imprudent to ask the
L448@P11: Americans for help, for if they were to refuse, it would be doubly difficult to change such a
L449@P11: decision at a later date. For this reason the British bided their time. But by the late Spring, it
L450@P11: was apparent that help would be needed if British oil stocks were not to be depleted to a
L451@P11: dangerous level by the end of the year. Assistance was sought from the Americans, who
L452@P11: proved extremely generous (particularly so, given their own straightened circumstances in
L453@P11: the Pacific theatre). By the end of June 45 tankers had been assigned to assist the British oil
L454@P11: imports and by mid-July 36 had sailed. This group was known as the “Red Gap”.40 The first
L455@P11: of these tankers to load in Houston, Texas and proceed independently at high speed across
L456@P11: the Atlantic, was the Ohio. She arrived in the Clyde on 21 June 1942.
L457@P11: As a fast tanker, Ohio was thus well placed geographically and operationally suited to meet
L458@P11: the needs of a fast tanker to accompany the 16-knot “Pedestal” convoy which was then
L459@P11: being planned in detail in the Admiralty. There was some disquiet about this plan, however,

L478@P12: Operation “Pedestal” – The Results
L479@P12: Effect on the Middle East and Mediterranean Theatre
L480@P12: The most significant outcome of “Pedestal” was well captured by a joint RN/RAF historical
L481@P12: study conducted in the autumn of 1950 in which it was observed that:
L482@P12: The cost of Operation “Pedestal” was very high indeed, as was to be expected with a
L483@P12: convoy of such vital consequence to the future of the Axis forces in the Mediterranean
L484@P12: being run for days on end within easy reach of enemy land-based aircraft. …
L485@P12: The arrival of the tanker Ohio at Malta meant that the island’s gravely depleted stocks of
L486@P12: aviation petrol could be replenished. The effect was immediate. Two days later, a
L487@P12: success against Rommel’s supply line was scored when the Rosolinao Pilo (8,326 tons)
L488@P12: was crippled by Malta-based Beauforts and was subsequently sunk by a British
L489@P12: submarine, by the light of flares dropped by a Wellington aircraft. …
L490@P12: The Battle of Alam el Halfa was launched on the night of 30/31 August 1942, with the two
L491@P12: German Panzer Divisions holding only 20% of their necessary supplies of fuel. By the
L492@P12: morning of 2 September Rommel’s offensive had been paralysed by shortage of petrol.
L493@P12: …On 7 September, a message was sent from the Deputy Chief of the German Naval
L494@P12: Command in Italy to the Chief of the Naval Staff:
L495@P12: “There is no doubt that, towards the end, continuation of the offensive in North
L496@P12: Africa collapsed because of inadequate supply services. The fear that this would
L497@P12: happen has unfortunately been realised.
L498@P12: After the offensive had been broken off, it depends on the supply question whether
L499@P12: the Panzer Army will be capable of holding their own, even on the defensive, in
L500@P12: face of the ever-increasing enemy…. The supply problem must therefore be
L501@P12: solved at all costs…. Even if we can increase the defences against submarines,
L502@P12: we have no means at our disposal at present to meet the far-superior abilities of
L503@P12: the RAF in night operations at sea. This last danger has grown to such an extent
L504@P12: that it must lead to a catastrophe, if no relief is found. I see to-day more clearly
L505@P12: than ever before that there can be only one possibility and that is by a strategic
L506@P12: offensive. The RAF in the Mediterranean, i.e. in Malta, must be eliminated. Fresh
L507@P12: operations must be launched immediately in this area….”43

L522@P13: the day of the Allied Landings in North Africa, till 13 May 1943, when the campaign
L523@P13: ended.
L524@P13: During this period 26% of the supplies sailing have been sunk or turned back through

L526@P13: January and February 23% and 21%, after that sinkings rose to 37% in March, 45%
L527@P13: in April and 78% in May. …

L534@P13: [Smaller proportions were carried by Italian aircraft]….44
L535@P13: In the lecture, Bullard also noted that while the air offensive against the Axis communications
L536@P13: was conducted by aircraft from several theatres, just under half (45%) were from Malta and
L537@P13: these sank half of the enemy shipping.
L538@P13: Operation “Pedestal” did not, however, achieve the long-term salvation of Malta and the
L539@P13: Governor continued to press for further re-supply. He was probably unaware of the precise
L540@P13: timing of the Allied landings in North West Africa, Operation “Torch” planned for early
L541@P13: November 1942. Still worried over the continuing drain on the Island’s supplies, he signalled
L542@P13: just over a month after the arrival of “Pedestal” that what he needed were:
L543@P13: Only absolutely essential articles of food and fuel…with small allocation of civil and
L544@P13: service stores.
L545@P13: The ‘Object,’ he added
L546@P13: …would be to put off target date until early January.
L547@P13: 45
L548@P13: The parallel assessment outline above from the enemy is most telling. The stalling of
L549@P13: Rommel’s offensive due to a lack of supplies, gave time for the final build-up of British forces
L550@P13: opposite the Afrika Korps and, then, for the opening of the Battle of El Alamein which
L551@P13: opened on 23 October 1942 and led to the clearance of Rommel’s forces from the Western
L552@P13: Desert. Further westwards, other, greater, events were also moving to a climax. The
L553@P13: continued starvation of supplies for Axis forces in North Africa in which Malta’s striking forces
L554@P13: played a major part, helped the subsequent Allied invasion in Morocco and Algeria –
L555@P13: Operation “Torch” which took place on 8 November 1942.
L556@P13: Once the Allied forces landed during “Torch” had taken Tunisia and had joined up with the
L557@P13: Eighth Army advancing from the east after the Battle of El Alamein had cleared the North
L558@P13: African coast, the safety of Malta was at last guaranteed.

L563@P14: Protection of a Naval Force in a Multi-Threat Environment
L564@P14: Operation “Pedestal”, along with the other convoys run through to Malta were all made in a
L565@P14: multi-threat environment. Some six months after the operation, the Naval Staff concluded
L566@P14: that:
L567@P14: Operation “Pedestal” demonstrated conclusively the great strides made in fleet fighter
L568@P14: direction with large numbers of fighters, and the experience so gained proved invaluable.
L569@P14: It proved, that, in case of necessity, and given reasonable conditions, a fleet could, by its
L570@P14: own efforts, force a passage through narrow waters in the face of very heavy enemy air
L571@P14: opposition.46
L572@P14: This point was later expanded in the (unpublished) Naval Staff History on Naval Aviation, in
L573@P14: which the Historical Section of the Naval Staff drew the conclusion that:
L574@P14: Operation “Pedestal” provides an example of the effectiveness of the fighter protection
L575@P14: so provided, and also of the disastrous results accruing from lack of it and the break up
L576@P14: of the convoy formation. The very heavy air attacks from Sardinia by over 100 escorted
L577@P14: bombers throughout daylight hours of 12 August, when the convoy was protected by a
L578@P14: total of 60 carrier-borne fighters, only succeeded in damaging one merchant ships and
L579@P14: two of the escorting ships. The [FAA] fighters attacking at a distance from the convoy
L580@P14: were usually able to break up the enemy formations sufficiently for the A/A guns of escort
L581@P14: and convoy to be able to deal with those that got through. That evening, after the carriers
L582@P14: had withdrawn and when the convoy, in some disorder after the submarine attack which
L583@P14: robbed it of both its fighter direction ships (one of them it’s A/A ship), was protected in
L584@P14: the air by only six Beaufighters, about 20 Ju88s hit three merchant ships with torpedoes.
L585@P14: The convoy then became completely disorganised; five stragglers (in addition to HMS
L586@P14: Manchester) fell victims to MTBs. Three merchant ships in convoy were hit by bombs
L587@P14: next morning while there was still no fighter direction; and ships which had become
L588@P14: detached suffered further damage in the course of the day.47
L589@P14: The other convoys which were conducted in a multi-threat were those through the Arctic to
L590@P14: Russia. Similarities and differences have been noted.
L591@P14: Perhaps the most striking similarity between the Arctic and Mediterranean convoys was
L592@P14: that they both had to face multiple, and sometimes simultaneous, threats from air,
L593@P14: surface and subsurface enemies. Of these threats, that from the air proved in both areas
L594@P14: to be the single most deadly attack: the proportion of ships sunk by aircraft was 81% in
L595@P14: the Mediterranean and 55% in the Arctic (where enemy aircraft had further to fly, in
L596@P14: worse weather conditions, and without fighter protection). The effect from the other
L597@P14: threats on the convoys in the two areas, however, was not the same. A third of the ships
L598@P14: sunk in the Arctic were due to U-boat action, but submarines sank none in the
L599@P14: Mediterranean convoys. Nearly a fifth of the sinkings in the Mediterranean were caused
L600@P14: by motor torpedo boats but none of these craft operated in far northern waters. Mines,
L601@P14: too, posed a constant threat in both theatres, though they caused relatively few
L602@P14: casualties. During the period where these two Battle Summaries overlap, the losses in
L603@P14: warships was heavier in the Mediterranean convoy operations, though a heavy toll was
L604@P14: taken of anti-submarine escorts towards the end of the war in the Arctic when U-boats
L605@P14: were able to counter attack with homing torpedoes.48
